questions.q: What's the key difference between simple CASE and searched CASE?
options: Searched CASE lets each WHEN hold a full condition, not just an exact-match value
Searched CASE cannot use ELSE
Simple CASE can test multiple columns; searched CASE cannot
There is no real difference
questions.explain: Simple CASE tests one value for exact matches; searched CASE evaluates a full boolean condition per WHEN.

questions.q: In what order does SQL Server evaluate WHEN branches?
options: Top to bottom, stopping at the first match
Bottom to top
All branches simultaneously, picking the most specific
In alphabetical order of the condition
questions.explain: The first WHEN that evaluates true wins — everything after it is skipped for that row.

questions.q: Why does branch order matter in a searched CASE?
options: A broad condition placed before a narrower one can catch rows that should have matched the narrower one
SQL Server sorts branches automatically, so order never matters
Order only matters when using ELSE
It affects performance but never changes the result
questions.explain: Placing 'ListPrice < 500' before 'ListPrice < 50' means cheap products never reach the more specific Budget branch.

questions.q: Can a single WHEN in a searched CASE combine multiple conditions?
options: Yes, using AND/OR just like any boolean condition
No, each WHEN can only test one column
Only if using the simple CASE form
Only inside a stored procedure
questions.explain: WHEN ListPrice > 1000 AND Color = 'Red' THEN ... is valid — searched CASE conditions can be as complex as needed.

questions.q: When should you reach for simple CASE instead of searched CASE?
options: When testing one column for exact matches, like a color name
Whenever ranges or comparisons are involved
Simple CASE should never be used
Only inside a WHERE clause
questions.explain: Simple CASE is the more concise choice for single-column exact-match logic; searched CASE handles everything else.
